problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict:**  
I have found a complete solution. The minimum number of rectangular tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there is a bijection  
   \[
   \pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\},\qquad n=2025,
   \]  
   and the uncovered squares are \((i,\pi(i))\).

2. **Decomposition into two staircases.**  
   For each row \(i\) let  
   \[
   L_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<\pi(i)\},\qquad   
   R_i=\{(i,j)\mid \pi(i)<j\le n\}.
   \]  
   The sets \(L=\bigcup_i L_i\) (left of the holes) and \(R=\bigcup_i R_i\) (right of the holes) are disjoint and together contain all covered cells.

3. **Shape of the left region.**  
   The numbers \(|L_i|=\pi(i)-1\) are a permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  
   After re‑ordering the rows so that \(|L_i|\) is non‑increasing, the picture of \(L\) becomes the Ferrers (staircase) diagram whose \(k\)-th row from the top contains exactly \(n-k\) cells.  
   The right region \(R\) is the mirror image of this staircase.

4. **Lower bound for each staircase.**  

   *Lemma.* In a Ferrers diagram whose row lengths are strictly decreasing, any axis‑aligned rectangle contained in the diagram has width \(1\).  

   *Proof.* Suppose a rectangle occupies columns \(c,\dots ,c+w-1\) with \(w\ge2\) and rows \(r,\dots ,s\) with \(r<s\). Because the row lengths drop by at least one when moving from row \(r\) to row \(r+1\), column \(c+1\) belongs to row \(r\) but not to row \(r+1\); consequently the rectangle would contain a cell that is not part of the diagram – a contradiction. ∎  

   The left staircase contains cells in every column \(1,2,\dots ,n-1\). Since each rectangle can use only one column, at least \(n-1\) rectangles are necessary to tile \(L\). The same argument gives at least \(n-1\) rectangles for \(R\). Hence any tiling of the whole board needs at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]  
   tiles.

5. **Construction attaining the bound (identity permutation).**  

   Choose the permutation \(\pi(i)=i\) (the main diagonal).  
   *Left region.* It consists of all cells \((i,j)\) with \(j<i\).  
   For each column \(c\;(1\le c\le n-1)\) consider the vertical rectangle  

   \[
   T_c^{L}= \{(i,c)\mid i=c+1,\dots ,n\}.
   \]  

   In the identity permutation column \(c\) appears exactly in rows \(c+1,\dots ,n\), which are consecutive; thus \(T_c^{L}\) is a legitimate rectangle. The family \(\{T_c^{L}\}_{c=1}^{n-1}\) partitions the left region, using \(n-1\) tiles.

   *Right region.* It consists of all cells \((i,j)\) with \(j>i\).  
   For each column \(c\;(2\le c\le n)\) define  

   \[
   T_c^{R}= \{(i,c)\mid i=1,\dots ,c-1\},
   \]  

   a vertical rectangle covering exactly the rows where column \(c\) lies to the right of the hole. These \(n-1\) rectangles partition the right region.

   Altogether we have \( (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) non‑overlapping rectangles covering every cell except the \(n\) uncovered squares.

6. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower bound \(2n-2\) and the explicit construction both give the same number, so the minimum possible number of tiles is exactly \(2n-2\).  
   For \(n=2025\),

   \[
   2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
   \]

   Hence the answer is \(\boxed{4048}\).

---

### Detailed Solution ###  

Let \(n=2025\).  Index the unit squares of the \(n\times n\) board by ordered pairs \((r,c)\) with \(1\le r,c\le n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Uncovered squares form a permutation matrix  

Each row must contain exactly one uncovered square and each column must also contain exactly one uncovered square.  
Consequently there exists a bijection  

\[
\pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the set of uncovered squares is  

\[
U=\{(r,\pi(r))\mid r=1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Left and right regions  

For a fixed row \(r\) define  

\[
L_r=\{(r,c)\mid 1\le c<\pi(r)\},\qquad   
R_r=\{(r,c)\mid \pi(r)<c\le n\}.
\]

Set  

\[
L=\bigcup_{r=1}^{n}L_r,\qquad   
R=\bigcup_{r=1}^{n}R_r .
\]

\(L\) consists of all covered cells that lie **left** of the uncovered square in their row; \(R\) consists of all covered cells that lie **right** of the uncovered square.  
Clearly  

\[
L\cap R=\varnothing ,\qquad L\cup R\cup U=\{1,\dots ,n\}\times\{1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Shape of the left region  

The cardinalities \(|L_r|=\pi(r)-1\) are a permutation of the numbers \(0,1,\dots ,n-1\).  
Re‑order the rows so that  

\[
|L_{r_1}|\ge |L_{r_2}|\ge\cdots\ge |L_{r_n}|.
\]

After this re‑ordering the row lengths become  

\[
n-1,\;n-2,\;\dots ,\;1,\;0 .
\]

Thus \(L\) is exactly the Ferrers (staircase) diagram whose \(k\)-th row from the top contains the first \(n-k\) columns.  
The right region \(R\) is the mirror image of this staircase.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  A lower bound for tiling a staircase  

**Lemma.** In a Ferrers diagram whose row lengths are strictly decreasing, any axis‑aligned rectangle contained in the diagram has width \(1\).

*Proof.*  
Assume a rectangle \(Q\) of width \(w\ge2\) lies inside the diagram.  
Let its top row be \(p\) and its bottom row be \(q\) with \(p<q\).  
Because the row lengths drop by at least one when moving from row \(p\) to row \(p+1\), the second column of \(Q\) (i.e. column “leftmost + 1”) belongs to row \(p\) but not to row \(p+1\). Hence \(Q\) would contain a cell that is not part of the diagram, contradicting the assumption. ∎  

The left staircase contains cells in every column \(c\) with \(1\le c\le n-1\): for each such \(c\) there exists a row \(r\) with \(\pi(r)>c\) (because the set \(\{\pi(r)\}\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\)), and then \((r,c)\in L\).  
Since each rectangle can occupy only a single column, at least one rectangle is needed for each of the \(n-1\) columns, i.e.  

\[
\text{tiles covering }L\ge n-1 .
\]

The same reasoning applied to the right staircase yields  

\[
\text{tiles covering }R\ge n-1 .
\]

Therefore any tiling of the whole board uses at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]  

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Construction achieving the bound  

Choose the **identity permutation** \(\pi(i)=i\) (the uncovered squares lie on the main diagonal).  

*Left region.*  
It consists of all cells \((i,j)\) with \(j<i\).  
For each column \(c\) with \(1\le c\le n-1\) define  

\[
T_c^{L}= \{(i,c)\mid i=c+1,\dots ,n\}.
\]  

In the identity permutation column \(c\) appears precisely in rows \(c+1,\dots ,n\), which are consecutive; consequently \(T_c^{L}\) is a vertical rectangle of width 1 and height \(n-c\).  
The family \(\{T_c^{L}\}_{c=1}^{n-1}\) partitions the left region, using exactly \(n-1\) tiles.

*Right region.*  
It consists of all cells \((i,j)\) with \(j>i\).  
For each column \(c\) with \(2\le c\le n\) define  

\[
T_c^{R}= \{(i,c)\mid i=1,\dots ,c-1\}.
\]  

These are vertical rectangles of width 1 and height \(c-1\); they exactly cover the right region, again with \(n-1\) tiles.

All tiles are axis‑aligned, their interiors are pairwise disjoint, and together they cover every cell of the board except the \(n\) uncovered diagonal squares.  
The total number of tiles is  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  Minimality  

We have exhibited a tiling using \(2n-2\) tiles and proved that no tiling can use fewer than \(2n-2\) tiles.  Hence the minimum possible number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).

For the given board \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4050-2 = 4048 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Therefore the smallest number of rectangular tiles that Matilda can place is \(\boxed{4048}\).**
